tagline.text: A volcanic massif at the tip of the Bataan Peninsula and the Tarak Ridge hike

location.label: Location
location.text: Alas-asin, Mariveles, Bataan, the Tarak Ridge jump-off

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,200–1,500 (day hike by public transport, per person)

children.text: Mount Mariveles is a stratovolcano massif at the southern tip of the Bataan Peninsula, and its best-known route is the Tarak Ridge climb from Alas-asin, Mariveles. It is an intermediate-to-hard hike with the Papaya River, forest, and ridge views over Corregidor and Manila Bay.

Mount Mariveles is a stratovolcano and caldera complex at the southern tip of the Bataan Peninsula. Its height varies by source: Wikipedia gives 1,388 m in the text and 1,398 m in the infobox, and the summit caldera is about 4 km across. No historical eruptions are recorded, but radiocarbon dating points to an eruption around 2050 BCE, and the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) classifies it as "potentially active." The massif includes the Mariveles peak itself, Pantingan (locally Banayan Peak), Bataan Peak, Tarak Peak and Vintana Peak, while Mount Samat and Mount Limay are parasitic cones.

Most travelers come for Tarak Ridge on the western side. The jump-off is Barangay Alas-asin in Mariveles, and sources give the ridge at about 1,006 m and Tarak Peak at about 1,130 m. One local guide describes it as about 13.2 km round trip with about 975 m of elevation gain, and rates it 4–5 out of 9 (a major climb, trail class 3). From the top you get a broad view over Corregidor and nearby islands, Manila Bay and as far as Cavite.

The hike has three main stages. From the barangay hall to Nanay Cording's house takes about 30 minutes (about 1.5 km), from there to the Papaya River takes 2–3 hours, and from the river to the ridge takes 1.5–2 hours, the steepest part. Tarak Peak is about 30 minutes beyond the ridge. A day hike usually takes 10–13 hours round trip, and many people camp one night on the ridge. If you do not have the stamina for the whole climb, going only as far as the Papaya River is an option. Guides give the one-way time as 5–6 hours in one place and 6–6.5 hours in another, and a reader comment records about 2 hours from the ridge down to the Papaya River, so treat all times as estimates.

Guides say a guide and registration have recently become practically mandatory on the Alas-asin route. A 2026 guide gives a registration fee of about ₱50 per person at the barangay hall and about ₱1,000 per group (up to 5 people) for a guide, but the rules change every year. Check the latest notices from Mariveles tourism and the Bataan tourism office before you go.

A stream partway through the hike that serves as a rest stop and the last place to refill water. There is no water on the ridge, so fill 2–3 L here. Downstream villages use this water, so do not use soap in the river.

Where the forest ends, the ridge has a flat grassy area where you can pitch tents. However, strong winds off the South China Sea hit the ridge, and one guide warns that gusts can reach about 70 mph (about 110 km/h) and that fiberglass tent poles have snapped. It recommends aluminum-pole tents or pitching at the edge of the trees.
From the ridge you can see a panorama of about 270 degrees taking in the Bataan Peninsula, Corregidor Island, Manila Bay and as far as Cavite. On clear days the view carries far.

blocks.title: Tarak Peak and the mossy forest

children.text: About 30 minutes above the ridge, an optional route leads toward Tarak Peak and El Saco Peak. One trip report mentions a mossy forest near the summit.

The route to the Papaya River follows wide paths and grassland with strong sun. After that comes a steep forest climb where you pull yourself up by branches and roots. The grassland is burned for kaingin (slash-and-burn farming) in the dry season, so watch for brush fires in March and April.

Traverse routes run from Tarak Ridge toward Pantingan Peak or Vintana, and there is a record that the Ayala Mountaineering Club surveyed a Tarak Peak–Vintana traverse. Pantingan Peak is reached through Sitio Duhat in Saysain, Bagac.
The massif has hot springs such as Tiis, Saysain and Pucot. Mariveles Ridge is a separate route climbed through Sitio Parca. Both often require a local guide, so check beforehand.

items.title: Day hike
items.subtitle: Leave before dawn, descend before sunset

children.text: Take a Genesis or Bataan Transit bus bound for Mariveles from Cubao or Pasay in Manila. Guides say that leaving between 11 p.m. and 1 a.m. gets you near the jump-off at 3–4 a.m. Tell the conductor you are getting off at Alas-asin.
Register at the Alas-asin barangay hall and arrange a guide. On weekends a queue can form before 4 a.m.
Pass Nanay Cording's house and start the climb. There are no shops higher up, so carry water and food.
Reach the Papaya River, rest and refill water.
Climb the steep forest trail to Tarak Ridge and enjoy the view.
Have lunch and begin the descent. Guides say most injuries happen on the way down, so be careful.
Return to the Alas-asin jump-off. Plan to be back before 7 p.m.
Guides say the last bus to Manila leaves around 7 p.m. If you miss it, you may have to go to Balanga and look for a last bus there.
Leave Manila and travel to Alas-asin, Mariveles.
Register at the barangay hall and start hiking with your guide.
Have lunch and refill water at the Papaya River.
Reach the ridge and choose a spot sheltered from the wind to pitch your tent.
The next morning, watch the sunrise, have breakfast and break camp.
Descend and return to Alas-asin.
The ridge is known for rats, so seal your food and hang it up. Camping is not recommended in the rainy season.
Take a Genesis or Bataan Transit bus bound for Mariveles from Cubao or Pasay. It must be a Mariveles bus, not a Balanga one, and the fare is given as about
for a ride of 3–4 hours.
Older sources describe transferring to a minibus in Balanga to reach Alas-asin, but fares and routes may have changed.
The last bus to Manila leaves around 7 p.m., and if you miss it you may need to go to Balanga and look for a bus around 9 p.m.
Take NLEX and SCTEX, then follow Roman Superhighway into Mariveles.
Parking near the trail holds only about 5–8 cars, and guides mention nearby lots at about
per night.
One guide mentions the "1Bataan" ferry toward the Esplanade Seaside Terminal (MOA) as a way back, taking under about 2 hours at about
Ferry operations and schedules change often, so check before you leave.
Tricycles wait at the highway junction. Agree on the fare first and bring small bills.
The dry season from November to April is the most reliable. One guide names January as ideal, and warns that the heat on the lower sections is severe in April.

In March and April, kaingin fires can break out in the grassland and the sun is strong. In the May–October rainy season, camping on the ridge is not recommended, and the trail is slippery and dangerous after rain.
Within the day, start before dawn to avoid the midday heat. Guides give a sample schedule that starts hiking by 4:30 a.m., so you cross the sunny grassland while it is still cool.

Most people make a day trip or camp one night on the ridge, so few book lodging. If an overnight bus is hard, you can stay in Mariveles or Balanga town the night before and go to the jump-off before dawn.
Guides say there are no shops on the ridge and no vendors above Nanay Cording's, so bring all your water and food. After the hike, Mariveles town or Balanga are good for Filipino home cooking.

If you have time before or after the hike, you can add a trip from Mariveles harbor to Corregidor Island. One travel account describes two ways to go: a hydrofoil from Manila or renting a banca from Bataan. Spreading it over the day after your hike reduces the strain.
Register at the barangay hall and bring valid ID.
On weekends the registration queue can form before 4 a.m., so arrive early.
There is no water on the ridge, so fill 2–3 L at the Papaya River.
Seal your food and hang it up so rats cannot get to it.
Start between 5 and 6 a.m. before sunrise at the latest, and be back at the jump-off before 7 p.m.
The wind is strong, so bring extra tent pegs and tie down all gear.
There is no shade on the grassland sections, so you need a hat and sunscreen.
Guides say cell signal is available along most of the hike. Get a local contact number.
A 2008 guide said a typhoon in 2006 damaged the trail and one section needed a rope. Ask your guide about current trail conditions.
Guides say the first section is wide trail and grassland and very hot. Climb early in the morning to avoid the sun.

Guides say the Alas-asin route has become a semi-managed area where a guide and registration are close to mandatory, and rules and fees change often. Before you go, confirm the latest rules with the barangay hall and the Bataan tourism office.
Do not climb alone. Trails change after storms, and guides say a guide is essential.
Guides mention pit vipers in the woodland before the Papaya River, so watch the undergrowth.
Fiberglass tent poles have snapped in the strong ridge winds. Check your camping gear.
Brush fires from kaingin can occur in March and April, so turn back immediately if you see smoke or flames.
Guides say most injuries occur on the descent, so come down early while you still have energy.
Do not use soap in the Papaya River, and carry out all your trash.
